items.title: HPE posts $14.5B quarter with $5.7B of AI orders and says memory stays tight through late 2028. What server buyers should plan for
items.summary: The first of the four server makers accused of repricing signed contracts has reported, and its numbers show why: record AI orders, a $10.5B AI backlog, margins already drifting down, and a supply constraint the CEO now dates two years out.
items.content_html:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $14.5 billion on Monday evening, up 50% from a year earlier and 13% from the prior quarter, with adjusted earnings of $1.43 a share against the roughly $1.27 analysts expected. The Cloud & AI segment brought in $11.3 billion, up 69%, and networking $3.1 billion, up 12%. Orders rose 88% in the quarter. AI orders were $5.7 billion, split between $4.5 billion of AI systems and a record $1.2 billion of networking for AI, and the AI backlog left the year at $10.5 billion, more than 80% higher than a year ago.

For the full year HPE recorded $46.7 billion of revenue, $57.2 billion of orders and free cash flow of $4.5 billion, up 356%. Net leverage fell from 2.7x to 1.4x as the company paid down Juniper acquisition debt, and the Juniper synergy target for fiscal 2028 was raised from $450 million to $800 million. The dividend goes up 19% to 17 cents a quarter and the company plans about $3 billion of buybacks.

The number that matters for buyers

Chief executive Antonio Neri said on the call that supply of memory, NAND and other critical components is expected to remain constrained through at least the second half of calendar 2028. Chief financial officer Marie Myers described significant double-digit increases in commodity costs during fiscal 2026 and expects them to moderate, not reverse, in fiscal 2027. Gross margin was 38% for the quarter, up 180 basis points year on year but down 220 basis points from the third quarter, and management guided the Cloud & AI margin to about 14% for the year as the AI server mix rises and costs outpace pricing.

That is the context for the Financial Times report this site covered on Monday that HPE, Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro are asking customers to accept 25–45% increases on orders already signed as memory passes half of a server's bill of materials. Neither Neri nor Myers addressed repricing of signed contracts directly on the call; management said pricing remains disciplined. HPE had earlier said it rewrote quoting terms to allow adjustment for component costs, which is the mechanism those increases run through.

Guidance

For fiscal 2027 HPE expects revenue growth of 27–35%, non-GAAP earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 a share and free cash flow of at least $5.5 billion, with first-quarter revenue of $14.0 to $14.6 billion. Cloud & AI is guided to grow 30–40%, networking in the high teens to low twenties. The company also noted that 57% of its cumulative AI orders since fiscal 2023 came from sovereign and enterprise customers rather than hyperscalers, which is a different, more fragmented and more contract-sensitive buyer base.

The shares closed up 17.4% at $48.02 on Monday, lifted by the market-wide rally, then gave back 6.7% after hours as the margin outlook sank in. Dell reports on Tuesday evening and will face the same questions.

The counter-argument

Order growth of 88% and a doubling of AI systems orders say demand is not the problem, and a backlog that large gives HPE pricing leverage, not the other way round. The risk for HPE is less that customers walk than that memory makers capture the margin; the risk for customers is that they have no better option than to pay.

What to do

If you have a signed server order, ask for the component-cost clause in writing and the date the price was fixed. If you are planning fiscal 2027 capacity, budget for memory-driven increases through 2028 and compare the delivered cost per accelerator-hour with a reserved cloud commitment before signing. Watch Dell's call on Tuesday for whether it confirms the same constraint horizon; two vendors naming the same date is a market signal, not a negotiating tactic.

items.title: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 runs a 28-layer block twice per token: a 750B 'Loop Transformer' with a 1M context, no benchmarks, no API and no weights yet. What the looping trend means
items.summary: Three days after Thinking Machines looped Inkling 2 Mini's middle layers three times, Zhipu did the same to a 750-billion-parameter model, and the pattern says the next capability gains may come from reusing weights rather than adding them.
items.content_html:
Zhipu's Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on Sunday evening to subscribers of its GLM Coding Plan and users of its ZCode tool and Z.ai Chat, calling it the company's first Loop Transformer. The architecture keeps roughly 750 billion parameters but runs a 28-layer block in the middle of the network twice for every token, with 26 layers before it and 24 after, so the compute per token is that of a deeper model than the weights suggest. Z.ai claims the result is comparable to models of two to three trillion parameters. It has published no benchmarks for GLM-5.4 itself, only an ablation on a 30-billion-parameter model with the same design, which spent about 10% more compute and gained eight to eleven points on maths and science tests while producing 10–14% shorter answers.

The model accepts images for the first time in this line, a feature Z.ai pitches as visual coding, and the Claude Code model id carries a 1M suffix for the context window. Throughput is quoted at up to 200 tokens a second off peak and 70–80 at peak. Coding Plan subscribers get 50% more weekly quota on 5.4 than on 5.3. The API is promised after safety evaluation, with no date and no price; open weights are promised after what Z.ai calls safety hardening, again with no date. GLM-5.3 remains the newest model on Z.ai's API price list at $1.40 per million input tokens, $4.40 output and $0.26 cached. Z.ai also warns that 5.4 can fall into excessively long reasoning on some prompts, and says a significantly larger model is coming.

Why looping, and why now

Layer looping is not new in the literature, but November 2026 is the month it reached production from two directions. Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini, released on Friday and covered here on Monday, stores 24 layers and applies 48 by running its two middle blocks three times, which is how a 26.4-billion-parameter checkpoint fits in 20 gigabytes and runs on a laptop. GLM-5.4 applies the same idea at frontier scale and, notably, by converting an already trained dense base through continued training rather than pretraining a looped model from scratch. Per-token gates control how much of the second pass is written back, and the second pass reuses the first pass's key-value cache and sparse-attention indices, so the memory cost of the loop is small even though the compute cost is not.

The economic logic is simple. High-bandwidth memory is the scarcest component in the industry; HPE said on Monday night that memory stays constrained through late 2028. Looping buys capability with FLOPs instead of with parameters that must sit in that memory. Whether it buys enough is exactly what the missing GLM-5.4 benchmarks would tell us.

The counter-argument

A 30B ablation is not a 750B result, and shorter answers can mean better calibration or can mean a model that stops early. Until Z.ai publishes GLM-5.4 scores on the usual coding and agentic suites, the comparison to multi-trillion-parameter models is marketing. The lack of an API also means independent evaluators cannot run their own tests, and the weights that would let the open-source community verify the conversion recipe are not out.

What to watch

Three things would move this from interesting to important: published benchmarks for GLM-5.4, API pricing that shows whether the extra compute is passed through to customers, and the weights. If Z.ai prices 5.4 near 5.3 despite doubling the middle-block compute, it is subsidising the loop; if it prices higher, buyers will compare cost per task against Gemini 4 Hydrogen and GPT-6.2 Sol, both of which list at or below $2 per million input tokens. For teams already on the Coding Plan, the practical test is a week of real tickets with the thinking budget capped.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude Ship puts an agent on the whole pull request: PR Steward fixes CI, Approvals can merge-approve, and /ship opens the PR. What engineering leads should configure first
items.summary: Code Review was the easy part; the new beta lets an agent act on the findings and, under a policy file you write, approve routine changes without a human, which makes the policy file the most important code in your repo.
items.content_html:
Anthropic on Monday bundled three GitHub-native capabilities into a beta it calls Claude Ship. Code Review, generally available since October 15, reads a pull request and posts findings. PR Steward, new and in beta, acts on them: it fixes failing CI checks, resolves merge conflicts, responds to reviewer comments, and after every push leaves a comment explaining what changed and how to roll it back. Claude Approvals, also beta, applies an approval policy written in plain language and stored in the repository, and can approve routine changes or escalate them to named humans. A new /ship command in the Claude Code CLI and desktop app chains the lot: push, open the PR, review, iterate until checks pass.

Availability is Claude Team and Enterprise on GitHub repositories only. Organisations with zero-data-retention, HIPAA or customer-managed-key configurations are excluded for now. Review and Steward are billed on token usage under admin-set monthly limits; /ship counts toward normal Claude Code usage. Eligible Enterprise customers can claim at least $10,000 of Claude Ship credits until January 15, 2027.

The boundaries Anthropic drew

PR Steward cannot approve or merge. Claude Approvals can approve, but only within the policy file, which takes effect once it is on the default branch, and GitHub branch protection still applies on top. Anthropic recommends starting in observe-only mode on a single repository with a spend limit, and says the policy can take Code Review findings and custom classifiers as inputs. A developer steers the agent with @claude in PR comments and stops it with @claude stop. Anthropic's internal evidence is that merged pull requests on the Claude Code team more than doubled from June to September while the share of reverted PRs fell by more than 40%; the company quotes itself, so treat it as a vendor claim.

Why the policy file is the real product

This is the first mainstream release in which an agent's output can satisfy a required review on a protected branch. In GitHub's model, a required approval is a security control; CODEOWNERS and branch protection exist to keep a single compromised account from shipping code alone. A natural-language policy that auto-approves, say, dependency bumps and documentation changes is reasonable. The same file with a loosely worded clause is a path from a prompt injection in a PR description to an approved merge. The site's security coverage of the last fortnight, the Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI poisoning and the Together AI credential leak, both started with an agent doing something plausible inside a repository.

The counter-argument

Teams already run auto-merge for Dependabot and have for years; the novelty is scope, not kind. And the alternative to agent approval is review queues that stretch for days while agents write most of the code, which is the situation Anthropic says it was in. The question is not whether to allow it but what is routine enough to allow.

What to do

Enable Code Review only for the first two weeks and measure how many findings reviewers act on. Add PR Steward on one repository with a monthly cap and watch the rollback comments; they are the audit trail. Before you turn on Approvals, put the policy file under CODEOWNERS, require two human reviews for changes to it, keep the GitHub rule that a human approval is still required on anything touching auth, payments or infrastructure, and run observe-only mode until you can list what the agent would have approved and agree with every line. Then expand by file path, not by repository.

Amazon has worked with Decart on Trainium performance since 2025 and says the goal is faster, cheaper training and inference on its own silicon, which Andy Jassy expects to sell externally as a significant business. Separately the New York Times reported that Musk told SpaceX staff in August the company could not compete in AI and renamed an engineering chat 'Sell compute because we can't compete'; Anthropic's prospectus shows it reserving all of Colossus 1 at up to $3.1 billion a month once fully delivered, and Google contracted about 110,000 GPUs from June.

HPE reports $14.5 billion fourth-quarter revenue, up 50%, with $5.7 billion of AI orders and a $10.5 billion AI backlog; CEO Antonio Neri says memory and NAND stay constrained through at least the second half of 2028; shares +17% then −7% after hours
Cloud & AI revenue rose 69% to $11.3 billion and orders grew 88% in the quarter, but gross margin slipped 220 basis points from the prior quarter and the Cloud & AI margin is guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027 as AI server mix rises and component costs outrun pricing. Full-year revenue was a record $46.7 billion with free cash flow of $4.5 billion, and the fiscal 2027 guide is 27–35% growth. Management did not address the reported repricing of signed contracts directly; the Juniper synergy target rose to $800 million. Dell reports on Tuesday evening.

Z.ai releases GLM-5.4, a roughly 750B 'Loop Transformer' that runs a 28-layer block twice per token, with image input and a 1M context, to Coding Plan subscribers only: no benchmarks, no API price and no weights yet
Z.ai converted the trained GLM-5 base through continued training rather than pretraining a looped model, with per-token gates controlling the second pass and the pass reusing the first pass's KV cache; it claims capability comparable to models of two to three trillion parameters but has published only a 30B ablation showing eight to eleven points of gain on maths and science for about 10% more compute. The release follows Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini, which loops its middle layers three times to fit in 20 GB. An API is promised after safety evaluation and weights after hardening, without dates; GLM-5.3 stays the API model at $1.40 / $4.40.

Google DeepMind uses teams of Gemini 4 agents and Lean 4 proofs to find quantum algorithms with formally verified correctness, cutting the computing cost of a fusion simulation 11.8x and a state-preparation routine 290x
Each problem got an independent team of agents whose proposals were checked in Lean before entering a shared notebook, with teams exchanging ideas every four hours; every result is a proved Hoare triple with resource bounds, checked by an independent comparator against frozen specifications, because the circuits cannot be tested classically or on current hardware. The blog reports the inertial-confinement-fusion computation falling from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits, a photochemistry problem 8x cheaper and a cytochrome P450 simulation 2.5x, with the Lean library and solutions open-sourced; the optimised circuits still exceed what the first error-corrected machines will offer.

Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX and xAI under consumer-protection law over Grok's sexualised images, citing a study that counted 3 million in eleven days and about 23,000 apparently of children; Virginia seeks up to $2,500 per wilful violation
Virginia filed in Richmond under its Consumer Protection Act and Oregon in Multnomah County under its Unlawful Trade Practices Act, arguing the companies marketed Grok as safe while promoting a 'spicy' mode that made abuse easy; neither brings criminal charges. The complaints cite the Center for Countering Digital Hate's count from late December to early January and more than 135,000 NCMEC reports from xAI and X since September 2025, over 90% initially unusable. SpaceX says such content is prohibited, safeguards have been strengthened and users circumvented restrictions.

Paradromics will run its brain-to-speech decoders on Nvidia Holoscan and edge hardware with a sub-10-millisecond target for direct speech and 100 ms for text-first pipelines; the Connexus implant remains in an FDA-approved early feasibility study
The Austin company's 2026 roadmap ports speech decoding and synthesis to Holoscan, profiles power, and ships Nvidia IGX systems to academic partners in its APEX programme; 2027 adds motor control and vision-language-action models, with the long-term goal of a wearable external computer. Online fine-tuning is meant to recalibrate the decoder in the background as neural signals drift. No financial terms were disclosed, Nvidia issued no separate release, and the first participant's phone call with her grandchildren, reported in September, remains the only published outcome.

Ant Group leads a $100 million round in Simplexity Robotics at a $1.6 billion valuation a year after founding; Zoox starts driverless rides in Los Angeles for employees only; Waymo files two NHTSA recalls with its freeway suspension still in force
Simplexity, founded by three ex-Li Auto executives, sells a wheeled humanoid that runs CNC machines to customers including a Tesla and Figure supplier, and showed a service robot called iX on Monday; Bloomberg notes Chinese firms shipped 97% of humanoids in the first three quarters of 2026 and the NDRC has warned of a bubble. Zoox's Santa Monica launch is its fifth market, with public riders deferred to 2027. Waymo's recalls cover driving in closed freeway lanes, remedy still in development, and response to manual traffic direction, already updated; it also paused Bay Area service for storms through Thanksgiving week.

items.title: Together AI confirms a coding agent leaked customer prompts; OpenRouter drops three providers and pulls zero-data-retention from 125 endpoints. What the canary experiment proved, and what to rotate
items.summary: A single credential committed by an AI coding agent, plus a five-month canary-token study, has turned 'zero data retention' from a checkbox into a claim you now have to test yourself.
items.content_html:
On Saturday Together AI published the kind of incident report that security teams had been expecting since the summer. An AI coding agent working inside the company committed a credential to Together's public GitHub repository, xorl. The credential opened a private Hugging Face repository that held samples of customer prompts, retained for software testing. Together's secret scanner caught the commit and it was reverted, but not before an unknown party downloaded the samples, searched them for secrets and began testing what they found. Five of the credentials they tested were canaries planted by Dragos, which is how the incident surfaced at all.

The affected requests were mostly to three open-weight models, MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6, on four days: June 24, July 4, July 8 and July 14. Together has not said how many prompts or customers were involved and says its review is continuing. It has brought in an outside forensics firm and law enforcement, moved to scoped short-lived credentials, added credential checks on every pull request, changed how its coding agents are allowed to work, and made zero data retention the default for new accounts. Existing customers have to switch it on themselves.

Why a canary study matters more than one breach

Together's disclosure is one node in a larger map drawn by Dragos. Over roughly five months its chief research officer, HD Moore, pushed about two million prompts through more than 2,000 inference routes, each carrying a unique URL and a disposable credential. Any later fetch of that URL, or use of that credential, is proof that the prompt was stored and read. The findings: attackers were actively pulling data from three unnamed hosting providers, one adversary appeared to have compromised two of them at once, and a Chinese AI lab fetched the secret URLs from about two-thirds of requests that had been marked no-data-collection. A stolen AWS key traced back to a request that was flagged zero-retention. Dragos names no vendors; the companies are identifying themselves one at a time.

OpenRouter is the second to do so. On Sunday it removed three inference providers from its marketplace and stripped zero-data-retention eligibility from 125 endpoints, some as a precaution, saying its own systems were not breached and that affected customers have been notified. Secondary reports name the three as AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake and say they had been forwarding MiniMax traffic to MiniMax's own API rather than hosting the model themselves; Novita's notice gives an exposure window from May 28 to November 11. OpenRouter has not confirmed those names.

The two failure modes

Read together, the incidents expose two different problems. The first is retention that nobody meant to be permanent: test fixtures, debug logs, prompt samples kept to reproduce a bug, then forgotten. Together's samples were four months old when they leaked. The second is routing opacity: a customer picking a US host for a Chinese open-weight model may have had the request forwarded to the model maker's API in another jurisdiction, with a zero-retention badge still showing. Neither is a model vulnerability. Both are supply-chain hygiene, and both are invisible from the buyer's side without instrumentation.

The counter-argument from providers is fair as far as it goes: open-weight models are cheap precisely because a thin layer of resellers competes on price, and the big first-party APIs have had their own retention controversies. But the Dragos numbers suggest the problem is wide, not isolated, and the remedy it demonstrates costs almost nothing.

What to do

Rotate any secret that could have appeared in a prompt sent through a third-party route since May, and add prompt-content scanning to your own gateway so secrets stop reaching models at all. Ask each router or host for the list of upstream providers per model and whether requests ever leave their infrastructure. Then plant your own canaries: a unique URL and a dead credential in a small fraction of production prompts, with alerting on any hit. Finally, if you use an AI coding agent, apply the same controls Together now applies to itself: short-lived scoped tokens, secret scanning on every PR, and no agent with write access to a public repository.

items.title: Tesla starts rolling out FSD v15 with a '25x better' safety claim and no baseline, the same weekend Waymo pulls its robotaxis off freeways nationwide. What the numbers do and do not show
items.summary: One company shipped a new vision encoder shared with its humanoid and declared the singularity; the other accepted a California order after construction-zone incidents. Only one of them published a method.
items.content_html:
Tesla began pushing Full Self-Driving version 15 to early-access owners on Saturday, with Elon Musk promising a wide release in December's holiday update. The release notes describe a new shared vision encoder, trained on internet video and used across the consumer cars, the Robotaxi fleet and the Optimus humanoid; a generative overhead rendering Tesla calls Reality View; end-to-end learned handling of the start and end of trips; parking that remembers your usual spot; and better detection of signs, small animals, debris, potholes and standing water. Initial availability is on the redesigned Model Y; older HW3 cars are excluded.

The claim

The line everyone repeated is Tesla's: 25x better handling of safety-critical cases. On Sunday Musk clarified that he meant twenty-five times, not twenty-five percent, and welcomed readers to the singularity. What neither Tesla nor Musk has published is the baseline. The notes do not say whether the comparison is against v14, against an earlier build, or against a fleet average; they give no mileage, no definition of a critical case and no methodology. Reports describing the figure as 25x versus v14 are inferring, not citing. A ratio with no denominator is marketing until the denominator appears, and Tesla's consumer product is not subject to the disengagement reporting that California requires of permitted autonomous testers.

The technically interesting part is the encoder. If one perception model now serves cars, robotaxis and a humanoid, then every mile the fleet drives becomes training signal for the robot, which is the argument Tesla has been making for Optimus for two years. Musk said on Friday that Optimus would give an unscripted demonstration within one to two months and on Sunday that the AI5 chip would go to Optimus before the cars. Those are checkable promises with dates.

Waymo's weekend

Waymo, meanwhile, pulled its robotaxis off freeways across every market it operates in after an order from California regulators, following incidents in construction zones and closed freeway lanes. The company said no collisions or injuries resulted from the closed-lane events and that a recall remedy is pending. Freeway service was the feature Waymo rolled out most recently, and taking it away everywhere rather than only in California suggests the fix is in software rather than in local mapping. Elsewhere in the same roundup: Zoox robotaxis are now bookable through Uber in Las Vegas, Tesla has 1,507 robotaxis registered in Texas against Waymo's 1,345, and Tesla has opened personal Cybercab pre-orders at $29,990 plus $299 a month.

The counter-argument

Tesla's defenders will say that a disengagement count is a poor safety metric too, that Waymo's own numbers are self-reported, and that a company shipping to hundreds of thousands of cars has data no regulator-permitted fleet of a few thousand can match. That is partly true. It is also why the absence of any published figure is the story: the fleet with the most data has chosen to release a multiplier and nothing else.

What to watch

Three things in the next six weeks. Whether Tesla's wide release in December comes with any definition of a critical intervention or any mileage figure; whether Waymo's recall filing with NHTSA describes the construction-zone failure and the remedy, which will tell you how long freeway service stays off; and whether the Optimus demonstration Musk promised happens on the timeline he gave. For robotics teams, the shared-encoder claim is the one to probe: if Tesla publishes anything on transfer from driving video to manipulation, it will be the most consequential robotics paper of the quarter.

items.title: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis, released only as Lean code; James Maynard puts it at '98 or 99 percent'. What has been checked, what has not, and why labs are now talking about limits
items.summary: A four-page note, a machine-checked proof nobody has yet read as prose, and a Navier–Stokes claim on the same day have pushed 'superintelligence' from marketing into the mouths of chief scientists.
items.content_html:
On Friday afternoon, one day after Anthropic's shares began trading, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by the company, posted a four-page note claiming a proof of the Riemann hypothesis developed with Claude. The note says the method also settles the generalised version, GRH, and includes a timeline compiled by Claude running from October 6 to November 16. What Alpöge released is not a paper. It is Lean code, a formal proof that a computer can check line by line, and a footnote says his own prose draft ran to roughly 250,000 pages. He denies the timing had anything to do with the IPO, and points out he used Claude in July to find a counterexample to a conjecture about Jacobians.

What has been checked

By Friday evening Andrew Sutherland at MIT had compiled the Lean independently, meaning the proof type-checks. The remaining mechanical step is an automated comparison confirming that the theorem as formalised is actually the Riemann hypothesis and not a subtly weaker statement; Elliot Glazer, who works on formal mathematics, said the formalised statement is in fact GRH. James Maynard, the Oxford number theorist and Fields medallist, told the New York Times he was 98 or 99 percent sure it was correct and that it would be a historic milestone if so, while warning that understanding why it works will take a lot of work. Terence Tao wrote that comprehension will take time. Brian Conrad at Stanford called the manner of release frankly completely outrageous, which is the sharpest expression of a widespread complaint: a proof nobody can read is not yet mathematics in the usual sense, even if a machine says it is true.

The same day, Tristan Buckmaster of NYU and Alpöge posted a claimed proof of finite-time blow-up for the unforced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations, another Millennium Prize problem, with a Lean package of about 600,000 lines. Buckmaster called the write-up unpolished and heavily LLM-assisted and said that after OpenAI's September claim on the forced case they could not risk waiting. A caveat applies: the numerical certificate the formal theorems depend on has not been released, only its hash.

The reaction that matters for the industry

Mathematicians will take months. The AI industry took a weekend. Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, posted on Sunday that superintelligence is arriving and that humanity should not accept a handover of society to AI. Elon Musk declared the singularity. More substantively, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay on Sunday arguing that pretraining perplexity, the model's error at predicting the next token, is a more durable measure of capability than saturating benchmarks, and proposing that labs commit not to train past a shared perplexity threshold until monitoring and understanding reach a concrete milestone. Sam Altman called it the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while. METR's quarterly update, released Friday, said the length of tasks models can complete is doubling roughly every 3.6 months and that public evidence cannot rule out a sharp acceleration in AI research itself.

The counter-argument is worth stating. A formally verified proof of a famous theorem is a capability demonstration, not evidence of autonomy; Alpöge drove the process for six weeks. Perplexity thresholds are easy to propose and hard to verify across labs with different tokenisers and data. And the loudest voices on Sunday all have products to sell.

What to watch

Three checks will settle the mathematics: the statement-equivalence check Sutherland was running, an audit of the Lean project for non-standard axioms or unproved assumptions, and the first human-readable extraction of the argument's core idea. For Navier–Stokes, the release of the numerical certificate. For the industry, whether any second lab endorses Pachocki's threshold idea in writing, and whether the perplexity numbers he cited, around 0.91 for GPT-4 and below 0.8 for today's frontier, get published with methodology. If they do, the site's benchmark explainer will need a new section.

items.title: OpenAI's new usage policy took effect Friday: routers and gateways need approval, outputs cannot train substitute models, 'protected reasoning' is off limits. What it means for anyone reselling or wrapping OpenAI models
items.summary: Written in October and live from November 20, the rules arrive in the same week that the router ecosystem it targets suffered its biggest data-exposure scandal.
items.content_html:
OpenAI's revised usage policies took effect on Friday, November 20, replacing the version dated October 29, 2025. The changes were posted to the company's changelog on October 21 with 30 days' notice and attracted little attention until Semafor reported on them last week. They matter now because the category they single out, routers, gateways and aggregators that give third parties direct access to OpenAI models, is the same category that spent the weekend explaining how customer prompts leaked through its providers.

What changed

Three provisions carry weight. First, any platform that offers third parties direct access to OpenAI models must obtain prior review and approval. First-party applications, where a developer uses the API inside its own product, are exempt. The policy names no companies; an outside lawyer quoted in coverage said OpenRouter is clearly in scope. Second, the policy bans using model outputs to produce training data or training signals for substitute models, and spells out that this includes rubrics, reinforcement-learning environments, labels and data filtering, whether done for yourself or on behalf of someone else. Earlier versions prohibited training competitors on outputs; this version closes the indirect routes that distillation pipelines actually use. Third, extracting what the policy calls protected reasoning, the hidden chain of thought behind reasoning models, is now explicitly barred.

Smaller changes round it out. Law enforcement joins the list of uses requiring approval, the high-stakes rule extends from advice to automated actions taken by agents, and a new section defines OpenAI-approved use exceptions, giving the company a formal channel to permit things the text otherwise forbids.

The context that makes it bite

The approval requirement reads differently after the weekend. Dragos's canary study and the disclosures from Together AI and OpenRouter showed that prompts marked zero-retention were being stored and read somewhere in the resale chain for open-weight models. OpenAI's models were not involved; its first-party API is not sold through those hosts. But its policy now gives it the right to decide which intermediaries may stand between it and a customer, and the exposure incidents make that right easier to defend. The distillation clause fits the same pattern: with export controls tightening around who may reach US frontier models, OpenAI has reasons beyond competition to show it is policing resale.

The counter-argument comes from the developers who built on routers precisely to avoid lock-in. An approval regime lets OpenAI slow or deny competitors' aggregation layers, and the distillation language is broad enough to chill legitimate evaluation work: building a rubric with a model and using it to grade another model's outputs is standard practice in research. OpenAI has said approved-use exceptions exist for such cases, but the burden of asking has shifted to the developer.

A price change in the same week

One more OpenAI change for developers to note: the public pricing page now lists GPT-6 Rosalind, the biomedical research model, at $10 per million input tokens and $50 output with $1 cached, a promotional rate through at least December 31. The tracker previously carried $15 / $75 from the model's launch page. We have updated the row; the page also confirms cached input at $0.40 for GPT-6.2 Astra and $0.10 for GPT-6.2 Sol, both unpublished when those models launched on Tuesday.

What to do

Map how OpenAI models reach your users. If customers bring their own prompts and choose models through you, read the platform definition and start the approval process now; access can be revoked for violations. Audit any pipeline that uses OpenAI outputs to build graders, labels or training environments for other models and either stop it or request an exception in writing. Check whether your contracts with intermediaries pass through OpenAI's terms, because they now must. And if you rely on a router for open-weight models too, apply the lesson from the Together and OpenRouter incidents regardless of what OpenAI's policy says: know which host serves each request, and plant canaries to prove it.

items.title: The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday and Nvidia 14% as the AI trade cracked; Anthropic closed a $93.5 billion IPO into the selloff. What the correction is pricing, and what Monday's futures say
items.summary: Three indices in correction, a VIX at its highest since April 2025 and a 90% chance of a December rate rise: the week's real question is whether the AI build-out can still be financed at these prices.
items.content_html:
Friday was the day the AI trade stopped getting the benefit of the doubt. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1,261 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617, its second-largest point fall on record, wiping out its gains for 2026. The S&P 500 lost 3.7% for a seventh straight losing session, its longest streak since February 2020, and ended the week down 8.6%. The Dow shed 950 points. All three indices now sit at least 10% below their highs, the textbook definition of a correction. The VIX closed at 35.89, its highest since April 2025. Nvidia fell 14.01% to $125.53.

What actually moved

No big company changed its guidance on Friday. What changed was the discount rate and the risk premium around a very concentrated trade. Philadelphia Fed president Anna Paulson said she was open to back-to-back rate rises and Governor Lisa Cook warned of falling behind inflation; prediction markets put the odds of a quarter-point increase at the December 9 meeting near 90%. On top of that sat a cluster of Nvidia-specific headlines: a Reuters report that SEC enforcement staff are examining the company's accounting, California's attorney general confirming an investigative subpoena, and the continuing fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation, with the former chief executive due before three House committees on December 1. Add President Trump's Thursday threat of tremendous penalties on companies building data centres abroad, and the market had several reasons to sell the most crowded position it owned.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered the administration's reading on Sunday: the Fed risks a policy mistake if it over-tightens, Democratic hostility to AI is spooking investors, and the industry has done a terrible job explaining itself. By Monday morning the tape had steadied, with Nasdaq 100 futures up about 3.3%, Nvidia indicated around 8% higher and Anthropic about 3% higher before the open.

Anthropic's timing

Anthropic's IPO closed on Friday in the middle of all this. The prospectus shows 980 million Class A shares sold at $83, 956.4 million of them by the company, with a 30-day option for the banks to buy up to 147 million more, all from the company. Secondary reports say the option was exercised in full, which takes the deal to 1.127 billion shares and about $93.5 billion of gross proceeds, roughly $91.6 billion of it to Anthropic. A separate $26 billion private placement of Class N shares at the same price came from Google and Nvidia at about $10 billion each, AMD at $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft at about $1 billion each and TSMC at $500 million. The prospectus estimates net proceeds of about $117 billion with the option exercised.

The shares closed their first day at $97.17, up 17%, then fell 8.5% on Friday to $88.91, still 7% above the offer price. Reuters reported on Sunday that the process itself was unusual: a 22-bank syndicate led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley earned more than half a billion dollars in fees, some banks were capped at four senior bankers, and core deal-team members signed six-month agreements not to work with OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek or Hugging Face. Anthropic and its banks declined to comment.

The counter-argument

Bulls will note that nothing in the AI demand picture changed: Oracle said on Friday that financing for its OpenAI contract is in place, Nvidia guided to $130 billion for the current quarter only last week, and corrections in 2024 and 2025 were buying opportunities. The bear case is that this build-out is now funded by bonds, leases and vendor financing whose cost just went up, and that purchase commitments of $390 billion at Nvidia and roughly $895 billion at Anthropic were sized for cheaper money.

What to watch

HPE reports after the close today and Dell, HP Inc, Workday and Autodesk on Tuesday; listen for AI server backlog and whether memory costs are being passed through. December 1 brings Huang's closed-door House interview, December 9 the Fed decision. And keep an eye on Anthropic's lock-up terms in the prospectus: early releases tied to price thresholds are now a live question rather than a formality.

items.title: OpenAI's MedChemBench puts GPT-6.2 Astra at 84.5% on medicinal-chemistry problems; Novartis's chief executive says AI will not cure cancer in a decade. Both are right, and here is what pharma should take from each
items.summary: A new benchmark shows models can reconstruct molecules and reason over published papers; the man who runs one of the world's largest drugmakers says the bottleneck is biology nobody understands yet.
items.content_html:
Two statements about AI and drug discovery landed within days of each other and appear to contradict. On Friday OpenAI published MedChemBench, a benchmark of 99 problems drawn from 117 published papers and patents covering 761 molecular structures, on which its newest model, GPT-6.2 Astra, earned 84.5% of the available credit. Over the weekend Vas Narasimhan, chief executive of Novartis and a member of Anthropic's board, told an interviewer that nobody should expect AI to cure cancer within five to ten years, because biology is understood far less well than language or code. Read carefully, the benchmark supports the chief executive.

What the benchmark measures

MedChemBench scores four things: rebuilding a molecular structure, including stereochemistry, from a textual description; reasoning from evidence in the source paper; ranking or selecting compounds; and predicting numerical properties, with partial credit for near misses. Models get one attempt, no tools, no feedback and no experiments. GPT-6.2 Astra scored 84.5% at its highest reasoning setting, GPT-6 Astra 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol 82.0%, GPT-6.1 Terra 75.1% and GPT-5.6 Sol 58.2%. The component breakdown is the useful part. GPT-6 Astra scored 95.4% on structure reconstruction and in one example rebuilt an 18-atom ring correctly ten times out of ten where the previous generation managed zero. On compound selection and numerical prediction it earned about half the available credit.

OpenAI's own caveats are unusually direct: models may have seen the source papers in training, the benchmark tests reasoning over published results rather than discovery of new ones, and the scores do not show that a model can find a drug or improve a decision in a laboratory. Only OpenAI models were tested and the page does not say whether the problem set will be released.

What the chief executive measures

Narasimhan's argument is about where time goes in drug development. Chemistry, the part models now do well, is a small share of a programme that typically runs about twelve years. Most of the time and most of the failures sit in biology: picking a target that matters in human disease, and then proving safety and efficacy in people. Those steps are limited by how little is known, not by how fast anyone can read. His realistic forecast is a cycle shortened toward eight years within a decade, with AI's near-term value in simulations, paperwork and letting scientists move faster through work they already do.

The counter-argument has money behind it. Isomorphic Labs raised $5 billion last week with no drug yet in a human, Dario Amodei has talked about compressing decades of progress into years, and Ant Group's health app released a 560-billion-parameter open-weight medical reasoning model on Sunday, with a smaller multimodal version and an evaluation platform backed by 29 institutions. Capability is clearly rising. The dispute is about which bottleneck it hits next.

What to watch

The test that would move this debate is prospective: a model-chosen compound series entering and clearing a Phase 1 trial, or a model-proposed target validated in animals, with the prediction registered in advance. None of the current benchmarks, including MedChemBench, is that test. Until one exists, treat high scores as evidence that models are becoming excellent medicinal-chemistry readers and assistants, which is valuable and billable, and treat cure timelines from either direction as opinion. For research leaders, the practical move is to pilot models on the reading-heavy work the benchmark actually measures, structure elucidation, literature synthesis, SAR summaries, and to insist that any discovery claim from a vendor comes with the wet-lab result attached.
